questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the defining features of performance management
questions.stem: Night log, Kettle Hill: the society committee says services are judged against delivery standards, and managers must report shortfalls at every quarterly review. Which practice is described here?

options.text: Performance management tied to targets that managers are held accountable for meeting
Performance management limited to spending totals reported once the financial year closes
options.misconception: assumes accountability is only retrospective accounting

options.text: Performance management in which staff are judged only on the outputs they personally control
options.misconception: believes judgement rests only on things managers directly control

options.text: Performance management in which the annual report simply lists the money that was spent
options.misconception: mistakes publication of spending figures for performance oversight

questions.explanation: Setting standards and reviewing progress against them is what makes this performance management. Year-end spending totals are retrospective accounting, and judging staff effort ignores the manager's own duty.
questions.hint: Think about who is held accountable for meeting standards.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret cost evidence on contracting out
questions.stem: Field notebook, Fairhaven: the municipal record shows 42 of 60 local services moved to private providers last year, and unit costs fell in 21 of them. What does that record show about savings?

options.text: All 42 outsourced services cut their costs, confirming that contracting out always saves money
options.misconception: assumes external provision always lowers costs

options.text: Costs fell in a little over a third of the contracted services, so savings were not general
Costs fell in a minority of cases, so contracting out cannot explain lower spending at all
options.misconception: treats part of the cost data as proof of total failure

options.text: The figures say nothing about costs because a sample of 42 services is too small
options.misconception: believes a sample under sixty cases is never informative

questions.explanation: Only 21 of the 42 contracted services recorded lower unit costs, so the result is mixed rather than a general saving. A single number cannot settle the case, but partial savings do not make contracting out ineffective.
questions.hint: Compare the count of cost falls with the count of contracts.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why particular practices count as good governance
questions.stem: From the ridge at Ardmore: our little group runs on rulebooks now, with an independent audit of the accounts, minutes read aloud, and conflicts declared before votes. Why is this called good governance?

answer.exemplar: The changes match good governance because they make the body's conduct open to scrutiny: financial accountability through independent audit, transparency through published minutes, and integrity through declared interests. Each control lets members verify decisions rather than trust personalities, which is the whole point of the principles.

questions.explanation: Accountability, transparency and integrity are the core elements of good governance, so the society's new checks match them. Mere record-keeping would not let anybody verify a decision.
questions.hint: Name the three pillars the society's checks correspond to.

questions.explanation: The total establishment of 1,200 minus the 480 promotion appointments leaves 720 posts filled by open external recruitment. The remainder, not the promoted group, is the open competition count.
questions.hint: Subtract the promoted posts from the total establishment.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the merit-based component of a staffing return

stimulus.body: The council's staffing return lists 2,400 senior civil service posts. Some were filled by open competitive examination, others by promotion of serving staff, and the rest were made without any competitive selection. The return asks the council to report how many posts were filled on merit.

questions.stem: Log of the society meeting, Kelso: the treasurer read out the staffing note below and asked which figure the council had to report. Which figure is the merit-based share?

options.text: The 1,180 appointments made through open competitive examination
options.misconception: counts one competitive route as the entire merit total

options.text: The 320 appointments made by promotion from the general grades
options.misconception: treats internal promotion as the same as open competitive entry

options.text: The 1,500 of 2,400 senior posts filled through competitive selection
The 900 posts filled without any published competitive selection
options.misconception: assumes appointments without competition still count as merit based

questions.explanation: Merit staffing means entry and promotion on competitive grounds, so 1,180 plus 320 gives 1,500 merit posts. Counting one route understates the total, and the 900 non-competitive posts fall outside merit staffing.
questions.hint: Add both competitive routes before dividing by all posts.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish conditional grants from other grant types
questions.stem: Cold clear night at Wrayburn: the grant letter says the district may keep four million only if it matches every pound from local funds, and the money is withdrawn when the match is missed. What kind of grant is this?

options.text: A categorical grant that funds a named service with no further conditions attached
options.misconception: thinks a named purpose removes the need for conditions

options.text: A block grant handed over with no reporting or matching requirement of any kind
options.misconception: believes a general allocation can carry a matching condition

options.text: A project grant that requires one off payment but no conditions in later years
options.misconception: confuses a single payment with continuing conditionality

options.text: A conditional grant that attaches spending conditions to the transfer of funds

questions.explanation: The letter ties payment to a matching requirement that can be withdrawn, which is what makes the grant conditional. Naming a service or making one payment does not create that withdrawal mechanism.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the money if the condition is broken.

questions.learningObjective: Classify review as diffuse or concentrated
questions.stem: Notebook page from Stanmere: the chart shows six ministries sharing scrutiny of one programme, and 90 percent of members sit on no scrutiny body at all. What does the chart suggest?

options.text: Review is diffuse, since most members take part in no committee scrutiny
Review is concentrated, because a small group of ministries holds all the scrutiny
options.misconception: infers concentration from the number of ministries involved

options.text: Review is concentrated, because the few involved ministries decide on their own
options.misconception: confuses the number of bodies with the number of participants

options.text: The chart proves that most members oppose scrutiny and prefer no committees
options.misconception: reads absence from committees as opposition to scrutiny

questions.explanation: Concentrated review means few participants scrutinise decisions, while diffuse review means many members take part. With 90 percent on no body, the pattern is diffuse rather than concentrated.
questions.hint: Compare how many members take part in scrutiny at all.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the binding force of constitutional precedent
questions.stem: Standing on the dunes at Bromley: the old case is read aloud as the reason the new dispute must be decided as it was, though the judges argue the facts differ. Why treat the earlier ruling as binding?

answer.exemplar: The earlier decision set the court's interpretation of the constitutional rule, so later cases are decided consistently with it. Precedent makes the law predictable and treats like cases alike, which is why the judges follow the earlier reasoning unless a higher court overrules it, even where the facts seem distinguishable.

questions.explanation: Precedent makes law predictable and treats like cases alike, which is why the earlier ruling binds. Judges may distinguish the facts, but they cannot simply abandon the rule already applied.
questions.hint: Name the value precedent gives to consistent treatment.

questions.hint: Add the original bench to the newly created seats.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Separate an indicator from its target and display

stimulus.body: The regional bulletin explains that every service is rated on four measures from 0 to 5, and the four ratings are combined into a single published score. Each service is also given a threshold it is expected to stay below, and scores are recalculated every quarter. A league table then places services against one another.

questions.stem: Letter to the society from Oakmere: the bulletin below sets out how services are scored. Which element is the indicator itself rather than its target?

options.text: The quarterly cycle after which every score is recalculated
options.misconception: treats the reporting schedule as the measure itself

options.text: The four ratings combined into a single published score
The threshold value that each service is expected to stay below
options.misconception: confuses the benchmark with the underlying measure

options.text: The league table that places the service against comparable services
options.misconception: mistakes the presentation of results for the indicator

questions.explanation: An indicator is the defined measure used to assess performance, here the ratings combined into one score. The quarterly cycle is timing, the threshold is a target, and the league table is presentation.
questions.hint: Distinguish the measure from its benchmark and its display.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what performance management requires of managers
questions.stem: Diary entry, Windermere: I wrote that what we want is not more paperwork but managers who know what good looks like and are called to account when they fall short. What does this describe?

answer.exemplar: The diarist names standards and accountability, the two elements that define performance management. questions.explanation: Standards plus accountability for shortfalls are the two defining elements of performance management. More paperwork would add neither targets nor scrutiny of results.
questions.hint: Look for targets and review, not added paperwork.

questions.stem: Society minutes, Tavistock: the minutes were circulated before the meeting. Which combination matches the principles the minutes record as being followed?

options.text: Rule of law and political neutrality, with electoral accountability left aside
options.misconception: assumes neutrality excludes holding officers to account

options.text: Transparency and efficiency, with integrity and accountability left aside
options.misconception: believes speed and openness replace ethical standards

options.text: Transparency, integrity, accountability and the rule of law
Effectiveness, efficiency and economy, with participation left aside
options.misconception: confuses managerial efficiency with the wider principles

questions.explanation: The minutes describe disclosure, declared interests, audit and decisions within legal rules: transparency, integrity, accountability and the rule of law. Efficiency is valued but is not what the minutes record.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise centralised administration in a description
questions.stem: Night report from Marlowe Point: all spending authority, all staff appointments and all grant approvals now sit in one ministry in the capital, and regional offices only carry out what they are told. What is this?

options.text: Decentralised administration, in which regional offices choose their own priorities
options.misconception: reads local delivery of decisions as local choice of them

options.text: Federal administration, in which regions hold constitutionally guaranteed powers
options.misconception: assumes any regional office implies a constitutional guarantee

options.text: Devolved administration, in which regions legislate for themselves under statute
options.misconception: mistakes administrative devolution for legislative power

options.text: Centralised administration, in which decisions and appointments stay at the centre

questions.explanation: Concentrating approval and appointments in the capital while regional offices only implement is centralisation. Regional delivery is not regional choice, and devolution would require decision-making power to move.
questions.hint: Ask who actually makes the decisions about money and staff.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of posts filled without competition
questions.stem: Atlas annotation, Redcar: the note records that 62.5 percent of senior officials in one ministry entered by open competitive examination, and promotion from within accounted for a further 12.5 percent. What share lacked competition entirely?

options.text: Twenty-five percent of senior posts were filled without competitive selection
Eighty-seven and a half percent of senior posts were filled competitively
options.misconception: adds the two competitive shares and the base together

options.text: Thirty-seven and a half percent of posts lacked competitive selection
options.misconception: subtracts the internal share instead of both competitive shares

options.text: Fifty percent of senior posts were filled without competitive selection
options.misconception: treats the leftover as a half by halving the total

questions.explanation: Competitive entry covers 62.5 plus 12.5 percent, which is 75 percent, leaving 25 percent filled without selection. The two competitive shares must be added, not subtracted.
questions.hint: Add the two competitive shares, then take the remainder.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes a grant conditional
questions.stem: Globe-side notes, Sallowby: the central office promised the county money for roads only if the county kept its own roads in good repair, and inspectors check each year. Why is the money called conditional?

answer.exemplar: The transfer is conditional because it depends on the county meeting a test the central office can verify and enforce. If the repair standard is not met, the money is withheld or withdrawn. Naming a purpose for the payment, as a categorical grant does, does not by itself attach a test that the recipient must pass.

questions.explanation: Conditionality means payment depends on compliance with a test the centre checks. Naming a purpose for the money is not the same as attaching an enforceable condition.
questions.hint: Focus on money that can be withheld if a test is failed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the legal effect of a constitutional precedent

stimulus.body: The notice explains that the court has already decided the meaning of the constitutional provision in an earlier dispute. Judges in the new case must apply that meaning to the facts now before them, though they may note where the facts differ from the earlier dispute.

questions.stem: Copy of a parish notice, Kellerton: the notice sets out the case that the judges have relied on. Which statement describes what the earlier ruling does?

options.text: It sets out the facts the earlier judges found, which later courts may distinguish
options.misconception: treats the earlier ruling as only a record of facts

options.text: It establishes the rule of law on the point, binding later similar cases
It transfers the earlier dispute into the court now hearing the new case
options.misconception: believes precedent moves the old dispute into the new case

options.text: It orders the parties in the new dispute to follow the earlier procedure
options.misconception: confuses binding precedent with a direction to the parties

questions.explanation: Precedent establishes the rule of law and binds later courts on the same point, which is what the notice relies on. Findings of fact can be distinguished, but the rule itself must be applied.
questions.hint: Separate the rule of law from the facts that were found.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what distinguishes court packing from expansion
questions.stem: Observing log, Cranleigh: a reform adds judges chosen by the current majority and enlarges the bench, with no change to the cases heard. Why call this packing rather than ordinary expansion?

options.text: Because the number of judges is fixed by law that the reform quietly disregards
options.misconception: claims the bench size is fixed by a constitutional rule

options.text: Because the reform removes judicial independence by taking over case selection
options.misconception: confuses appointments with control over which cases are heard

options.text: Because existing judges are displaced to change how cases will be decided
Because the reform is openly justified by rising caseloads in the courts
options.misconception: assumes workload explanations are always unprincipled

questions.explanation: Packing alters the composition of a court to change likely outcomes, and displacing sitting judges is the mechanism. A workload explanation describes ordinary expansion, and adding seats alone is not packing.
questions.hint: Ask what the change does to the judges already on the bench.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute a composite indicator from component ratings
questions.stem: Chart annotations, Netherfield: each service is rated on four measures from 0 to 5, and the ratings of 3, 4, 4 and 5 are combined into one published figure. What is that combined figure?

options.text: Three, because the lowest of the four ratings pulls the score down
options.misconception: picks the weakest rating instead of combining measures

options.text: Four and a quarter, because the four ratings are added and then halved
options.misconception: adds the ratings and divides by the wrong number

options.text: Five, because the highest rating sets the ceiling for the whole service
options.misconception: lets the best single rating stand for the whole score

options.text: Four, because the mean of the four ratings from 3 to 5 is four

questions.explanation: Adding 3, 4, 4 and 5 gives 16, and 16 divided by 4 ratings is 4. Taking the lowest or highest rating discards the other measures, and halving the total is not the rule for a mean.
questions.hint: Add the ratings, then divide by the number of ratings.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Analyse who sets standards when work is contracted out

questions.stem: Notice pinned in the hut, Yarwell: the notice below describes how the service will be delivered. What does it show about contracting out?

options.text: The authority still sets the standards while a private firm carries out the work
The authority has withdrawn entirely and the firm now sets its own standards
options.misconception: treats an outsourced service as an unregulated one

options.text: The firm has taken over setting standards and inspecting its own output
options.misconception: assumes outsourcing always transfers standard-setting power

options.text: No contractor is involved, since the notice describes routine weekend work
options.misconception: reads scheduled weekend work as contracted delivery

questions.explanation: The notice separates the funder and standard-setter from the deliverer, the usual shape of contracting out. The authority still sets standards, and carrying out work is not the same as setting them.
questions.hint: Check who writes the specification and who performs the work.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the principle breached by a governance failure
questions.stem: Recollections written in 1998, Pentland: I remember the treasurer resigning when the committee refused to publish the minutes, and the whole society changing its rules afterwards. Which principle did the committee breach?

options.text: The rule of law, because refusing to publish minutes altered the society's rules
options.misconception: links a disclosure failure to the alteration of rules

options.text: Transparency, because the refusal concealed the committee's decisions
Effectiveness, because the treasurer's resignation slowed the society's work
options.misconception: treats a speed problem as the main governance failure

options.misconception: assumes the breach concerned who was allowed to decide

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the distribution of decision-making authority

options.misconception: treats the largest single share as the whole

options.text: Authority is entirely regional, since the regions hold the second largest share
options.misconception: assumes the second largest share must be the whole

options.text: Authority is split, with decisions spread across three separate centres
Authority is shared only between the capital and the regions, not the boards
options.misconception: ignores joint boards as a distinct centre of decision

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish precedent from judicial discretion
questions.stem: Handbook extract, Yewtree: the extract says courts must follow earlier rulings on the same point of law unless a higher court has overruled them. What does this rule restrict?

options.text: It restricts the freedom of a later court to decide a case on a different legal basis
It restricts the power of parliament to change the law the courts apply
options.misconception: reads a judicial rule as a limit on legislative power

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the quality of a performance indicator
questions.stem: Weather sheet, Lindenhall: the sheet proposes a single score for each service, built from waiting time, complaints, staffing and inspection results. Why is one combined number harder to defend than several separate ones?

answer.exemplar: A single combined number hides the trade-offs inside it: a service could offset poor inspection results with short waiting times, and the score would not reveal that compensation. Separate indicators let users see which dimension is strong and which is weak, and they make the weighting rules visible so the figures can be challenged rather than simply accepted.

questions.explanation: A composite score can let a strong dimension mask a weak one, and it hides the weighting decisions inside the calculation. Separate indicators make both the performance and the weights open to challenge.
questions.hint: Think about what a combined score can hide from its users.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a performance management report

stimulus.body: The committee report notes that two of the three targets were met, that the third was missed by eleven per cent, and that managers must now set out a recovery plan before the next review. The report also records that staff turnover rose slightly in the unit responsible for the missed target.

questions.stem: Weekend summary, Applewhite: the report below describes how the service is being managed. What does the report show?

options.text: Punitive management, since the missed target has already been used to dismiss staff
options.misconception: infers dismissal where the report only notes turnover

options.text: Performance management in operation, with targets, review and a required recovery plan
A performance report with no management content, since no decision is recorded
options.misconception: does not treat a required recovery plan as a decision

options.text: Purely descriptive reporting, because the targets are drawn from last year's figures
options.misconception: assumes targets describe the past rather than a standard

questions.explanation: Targets, a review of results and a required recovery plan are the working parts of performance management. Nothing in the report mentions dismissal, and a required plan is a decision, not mere description.
questions.hint: Look for targets, review and a required next step.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the risks of contracting out
questions.stem: Site rule sheet, Caerlyn: the sheet warns that a contractor may cut costs by using fewer staff, and that quality then depends on the council writing enforceable standards and monitoring them. What risk does the sheet highlight?

options.text: The risk that government funding for the contract is cut in a later budget
options.misconception: focuses on the funding of the contract rather than its delivery

options.text: The risk that the contractor wins more work than it can properly manage
options.misconception: mistakes the scale of the contract for a quality risk

options.text: The risk that the contract ends early without a suitable replacement in place
options.misconception: treats contract length as the main source of danger

options.text: The risk that cost cutting degrades service quality unless standards are enforced

questions.explanation: Contractors have incentives to cut inputs, so quality can fall unless the authority specifies standards and enforces them. Funding, contract size and contract length are real issues but not the risk described.
questions.hint: Focus on what happens to service quality when costs fall.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of external scrutiny in governance
questions.stem: Seminar notes, Brackley: notes record that 84 percent of sampled spending decisions were approved with a published rationale, and that independent audit followed 60 of those 70 decisions. What do the figures suggest?

options.text: Both transparency and audit coverage are incomplete across the board
options.misconception: reads a high transparency figure as a low one

options.text: Transparency is fairly well established, but audit coverage is incomplete
Audit is thorough, but published rationales are rarely available to readers
options.misconception: inverts the transparency and audit figures

options.text: The figures are too small to say anything about either transparency or audit
options.misconception: believes any sample is too small to interpret

questions.explanation: With 84 percent of decisions carrying a published rationale, transparency is reasonably well established, but 60 of 70 audited decisions leaves ten decisions unexamined. Audit coverage is therefore partial rather than thorough.
questions.hint: Read the two percentages separately, then judge each practice.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the trade-offs of centralisation
questions.stem: Letter from the warden, Elmsworth: the warden writes that everything now passes through the capital, so rules are applied evenly, but local sites wait weeks for decisions they used to make themselves. How should the trade-off be read?

answer.exemplar: Centralisation buys uniformity of treatment, standard rules and a single point of accountability, which is why the equal application of rules is a genuine gain. The cost is delay, slower local responsiveness and reduced discretion for those closest to the work, so the arrangement is efficient for consistency rather than for speed.

questions.explanation: Centralisation delivers uniform application of rules and a single point of accountability, but it slows decisions and removes local discretion. Uniformity is a real gain even though responsiveness suffers.
questions.hint: Name the gain and the cost that the letter records.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a merit-based staffing percentage
questions.stem: Tally sheet, Kelpwick: the sheet records 900 civil service posts, of which 315 were filled through open competitive examination and internal promotion combined. What percentage of posts were filled on merit?
questions.explanation: The 315 merit appointments out of 900 posts is 0.35, that is 35 percent. The remainder of 585 posts were filled without competitive selection, which is the part the merit principle is concerned with.
questions.hint: Divide the competitively filled posts by the total number of posts.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a conditional grant from a recipient's viewpoint

stimulus.body: The bulletin explains that the region receives 4 million in central funding each year, but only if it maintains spending on the programme at no less than last year's level. The bulletin notes that inspectors check the accounts annually and that any shortfall in spending reduces the payment by the same amount.

questions.stem: Bulletin of the ratepayers, Dellwood: the bulletin below describes the funding arrangement. What does it tell the region?

options.text: The region must match the central payment with funds from its own budget
options.misconception: confuses a spending floor with a matching requirement

options.text: The payment is guaranteed in full regardless of how the region spends it
options.misconception: reads a conditional payment as an unconditional entitlement

options.text: The payment depends on maintaining the programme's spending at a stated floor
The region's grant is withdrawn entirely at the first inspection finding
options.misconception: assumes the whole grant lapses rather than being reduced

questions.explanation: The arrangement is conditional because the payment depends on holding spending at a stated floor, and the bulletin makes the penalty a reduction rather than total withdrawal. A matching requirement would need the region to find matching funds.
questions.hint: Check whether the condition is a floor, a match or a total ban.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of concentrated review
questions.stem: Committee minutes, Fordington: the minutes describe a single standing committee of nine members examining every budget line, with no other body involved. What does this arrangement produce?

options.text: Executive scrutiny, since the committee's findings go straight to the minister
options.misconception: confuses a legislature's committee with the executive

options.text: Diffuse review, in which many members take part in checking every decision
options.misconception: reads a single committee as wide participation

options.text: No scrutiny at all, since a committee cannot examine a budget on its own
options.misconception: assumes scrutiny needs several separate bodies

options.text: Concentrated review, in which one small group scrutinises decisions on behalf of all

questions.explanation: A single nine-member committee examining everything is concentrated review: few participants scrutinise decisions for the whole body. Wide participation would require many members involved across several bodies.
questions.hint: Count how many people are doing the checking.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the role of precedent in a dispute
questions.stem: Testimony summary, Hawkshaw: the summary records 40 appeals, 26 of which were resolved simply by applying an earlier ruling of the same panel, and 9 by distinguishing the facts. What do the numbers show?

options.text: Precedent settled few cases, since most appeals required fresh legal argument
options.misconception: reads 26 of 40 as a small minority

options.text: Precedent settled most cases, and distinguishing the facts was the next common route
Distinguishing the facts was the dominant method, with precedent used rarely
options.misconception: swaps the counts of the two methods used

options.text: Only five appeals were decided by either method, so precedent barely applied
options.misconception: adds the two methods as if they were the remainder

questions.explanation: Applying an earlier ruling resolved 26 of 40 appeals, and distinguishing the facts resolved a further 9, so precedent dominated with distinguishing as the main alternative. Only five appeals needed fresh argument.
questions.hint: Compare the two method counts with the total.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how packing changes judicial decisions
questions.stem: Diary of the committee, Prideaux: the diarist notes that the extra judges were all chosen by the government, that they sat on the most contested cases, and that the older judges withdrew from those hearings. What effect follows?

answer.exemplar: The effect follows from who occupies the court in the cases that matter. By filling the contested seats with judges chosen by the government and removing the sitting judges from those hearings, the composition of the panel in the sensitive cases is set by the government, so the rules of precedent may be applied in a way that favours the government position.

questions.explanation: Packing works through composition, so government-chosen judges deciding the contested cases, with the earlier judges removed, shifts how precedent is applied. Only the cases that matter are affected by who hears them.
questions.hint: Focus on which judges heard the cases that mattered.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate an indicator weighted by component scores
questions.stem: Scrapbook page, Quarrendon: the page gives a service four ratings of 3, 4, 4 and 5 out of 6, and the published indicator is the mean of those four ratings. What is the published indicator?
questions.explanation: The ratings total 16 and the mean of four ratings is 16 divided by 4, which is 4. Using a sum of 16 or the top rating of 5 would ignore how the indicator is defined.
questions.hint: Add the four ratings and divide by four.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply performance management to a practical scenario
questions.stem: Night summary, Ironvale: the service was asked to cut response times by a fifth this year, and the managers must report every quarter on whether they are meeting that target. What does the arrangement set in place?

options.text: A staffing exercise, since fewer staff are needed to meet the reduced times
options.misconception: assumes the target implies a particular staffing level

options.text: A budget exercise, since a fifth of the budget has been set aside for the service
options.misconception: reads a fifth of something as a funding share

options.text: A measurable target with a reporting duty, which is the core of performance management
A legal duty, since the target is written into the service's charter
options.misconception: presumes a target always carries legal force

questions.explanation: A target set in advance, measured on defined terms and reported regularly is exactly the performance management mechanism. Nothing in the description concerns budget shares, staffing levels or legal obligation.
questions.hint: Look for a standard, a measurement and a reporting duty.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Analyse cost data on contracted services
questions.stem: Memo from the treasurer, Tanfield: contracted services cost 8.2 million against 9.4 million in house, and internal managers spent 140,000 managing the contracts. What is the net saving?

options.text: There is no net saving, since contracting out always increases total spending
options.misconception: generalises a cost figure into a universal rule

options.text: The net saving is 1,200,000 with no further adjustment needed
options.misconception: ignores the cost of managing the contracts

options.text: The net saving is 1,340,000 after adding the management costs to savings
options.misconception: adds management costs instead of subtracting them

options.text: The net saving is 1,060,000 once management costs are deducted

questions.explanation: The gross saving of 1,200,000 falls to 1,060,000 once the 140,000 of contract management is deducted, because managing contracts is itself a cost of the arrangement. Adding that cost would overstate the benefit.
questions.hint: Deduct the cost of running the contracts from the gross saving.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why participation matters in good governance
questions.stem: Aunt's account of the election, Old Nettleton: she recalls that the committee had to justify each decision at a public meeting, that anyone could ask questions, and that her questions changed one decision. What made that good governance?

answer.exemplar: The combination of public decisions, questions from any member and a decision actually changed shows information flowing upward as well as downward. Accountability means the body can be asked to justify itself, transparency means the reasons are given in public, and participation means the answers affect what is decided.

questions.explanation: Public justification, questions from members and a decision changed together show accountability, transparency and participation in operation. Reporting results without a route for members to question them would omit the participation element.
questions.hint: Look for the direction information travelled in the account.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of decisions delegated locally
questions.stem: Account book entry, Trewin: 1,850 decisions were taken in the central ministry this year and 1,110 of them were taken centrally, with the rest delegated to regional offices. What percentage was delegated?
questions.explanation: The delegated decisions number 1,850 minus 1,110, which is 740, and 740 out of 1,850 is 0.40, that is 40 percent. Counting the centrally taken decisions instead would describe the opposite share.
questions.hint: Find the delegated count, then divide by all decisions taken.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a change in merit staffing over time

stimulus.body: The committee reports that in 1998 only 41 percent of senior civil service posts were filled through competitive selection, and that by 2018 the figure had risen to 63 percent. The committee notes that the rise followed the introduction of published competition rules and independent assessment of candidates.

questions.stem: Bulletin extract, Kelso: the extract below reports a staffing change. What does the extract show about merit staffing?

options.text: The merit share doubled between the two dates the committee compares
options.misconception: treats a 22 point rise as a doubling

options.text: The merit share rose by 22 percentage points after competition rules were introduced
The merit share fell, because independent assessment reduced competitive appointments
options.misconception: reads a rising figure as a falling one

options.text: The committee proves that competition rules always produce large improvements
options.misconception: generalises one case into a universal causal claim

questions.explanation: Competitive selection rose from 41 percent to 63 percent, an increase of 22 percentage points, following the introduction of competition rules. The figures describe one instance and do not prove a general rule about procedural reform.
questions.hint: Subtract the earlier percentage from the later one.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the effects of conditionality on recipients
questions.stem: Complaint slip, Oxenholme: the slip complains that the district is now asked to spend money it had planned for other things, because central funding for the road only arrives if the district repairs first. What feature of the scheme is at work?

options.text: The categorical grant, which ties the money to one named service with no test
options.misconception: believes a named purpose removes the need for a test

options.text: The block grant, which allows districts to spend freely once the money arrives
options.misconception: treats a conditional payment as an unrestricted allocation

options.text: The matching condition, which lets the centre shift spending priorities to the centre
options.misconception: confuses the condition with a transfer of spending control

options.text: The non-matching condition, which obliges the centre to fund the work first
options.misconception: reverses which side must find the money

questions.explanation: Because the transfer depends on the district's own spending, the scheme lets the centre influence local priorities. A block grant would leave spending free, and a categorical grant attaches no test to be failed.
questions.hint: Ask who must spend first before the money arrives.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a committee participation pattern
questions.stem: Working paper, Limehouse Rise: the paper records that 12 of 60 members sit on scrutiny committees, and that 9 of those 12 chairs a committee. What does the pattern indicate?

options.text: Scrutiny is absent, since no more than a fifth of members take any part
options.misconception: reads a minority of participants as no participation

options.text: Scrutiny is wide in membership and evenly led, since no committee has a chair
options.misconception: ignores the chairs recorded in the paper

options.text: Scrutiny is wide in membership but unled, since only 12 of 60 members attend
options.misconception: treats a small committee as broad participation

options.text: Scrutiny is narrow in membership but concentrated in leadership, since most chairs hold a post

questions.explanation: Twelve of 60 members take part, so participation is narrow, and nine of those twelve chair a committee, so leadership is concentrated among a small group. A minority of members participating still constitutes real scrutiny.
questions.hint: Read the membership figure and the leadership figure separately.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how precedent can be departed from
questions.stem: Court report reprint, Valewood: the reprint notes that a lower court felt obliged to follow an earlier ruling it considered wrong, and that the higher court could depart from it. What does the report show about precedent?

answer.exemplar: The report shows that the binding force of precedent is a matter of hierarchy rather than absolute correctness. A lower court must follow the earlier ruling even if it thinks the reasoning is faulty, because only a court above can overrule, so departures are made by a higher court and the law stays predictable while remaining capable of correction.

questions.explanation: Precedent binds through hierarchy, so a lower court follows a ruling it doubts while a higher court may overrule. Departure is therefore structured, which is what keeps the law predictable and correctable.
questions.hint: Ask which court may depart from the earlier ruling.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify weaknesses in a chosen indicator

stimulus.body: The bulletin announces that from this year services will be rated on the average time taken to answer a call, in minutes, with no adjustment for the difficulty of the cases handled. It notes that some units handle many more difficult cases than others, and that the figures will be published in a league table.

questions.stem: Bulletin header, Marbury: the header below announces a new indicator. What weakness does it contain?

options.text: It uses minutes rather than seconds, so the unit of measurement is unsuitable
options.misconception: treats the choice of unit as the real source of bias

options.text: It measures only the speed of answering, ignoring the difficulty of the cases handled
It publishes a league table, which exposes services to unfair comparison
options.misconception: blames the presentation rather than the measure

options.text: It replaces the previous indicator, so historic comparisons are no longer possible
options.misconception: treats a change of indicator as the key design weakness

questions.explanation: Without adjustment for case difficulty, the average time reflects the mix of cases as much as the service's efficiency. The unit, the league table and the change of measure are all secondary to that design weakness.
questions.hint: Ask what the average is made of besides the service's own speed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess how performance information supports accountability
questions.stem: Log fragment, Fernwick: managers spent 300 hours a quarter on performance reporting, while the number of documented service failures fell from 40 to 12 over the same year. What can the fragment support?

options.text: That the reporting hours were wasted, because failures fell despite them
options.misconception: treats a co-occurring decline as evidence of waste

options.text: That performance information caused the fall in failures, since the hours rose first
options.misconception: treats a plausible sequence as proof of causation

options.text: That performance information fell, which is consistent with better control of services
Nothing, because 300 hours of reporting is too much effort to be justified
options.misconception: judges the method on effort alone rather than outcome

questions.explanation: Failures fell from 40 to 12 while the reporting effort continued, which is consistent with the information supporting better control. The figures show a pattern, not a proven causal link, and the hours are not wasted while failures fall.
questions.hint: Note what the figures cannot establish, and what they are consistent with.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the case for contracting out
questions.stem: Officer handover notes, Bexley: the notes say the contractor now provides the service more cheaply, that the council still checks the work twice a year, and that residents report the service is no less reliable. What do the notes support?

answer.exemplar: The notes support the case for contracting out on these facts: the service is cheaper, the authority retains inspection, and users report no loss of reliability. questions.learningObjective: Describe the features of a centralised system

options.misconception: assumes local reporting implies local discretion

questions.learningObjective: Explain why merit staffing is contested
questions.stem: Remembrance, Marchmont: the writer recalls that when posts were advertised openly the appointees were often unknown to the networks of the service, and the older staff complained that the standard had fallen. How should the principle be assessed?

options.text: Open competition lowers standards because it ignores the service's internal networks
options.misconception: takes a complaint about unfamiliarity as a quality judgement

options.text: Open competition widens the pool and sets a standard, though networks may resist it
Internal promotion is superior because it guarantees the same standard every time
options.misconception: assumes any familiar choice guarantees consistent quality

options.text: The merit principle matters only where posts are numerous enough to be competitive
options.misconception: believes the principle applies only to large intakes

questions.explanation: Open competition widens the recruitment pool and applies a published standard, so the principle favours it. Existing networks may object to unfamiliar appointees, but unfamiliarity is not itself evidence of lower quality.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the funding left after conditionality
questions.stem: Radio transcript, Stanmere: the transcript says a region was offered 200,000 in support, but spending 250,000 on the scheme cut the payment by 100,000 because the condition was missed. What is the net support the region receives?

options.misconception: adds a penalty to the payment instead of deducting it

options.text: The region receives 200,000, since the penalty is charged to the next year's budget
options.misconception: assumes the penalty falls in a later period

options.text: The region receives 100,000, because the 100,000 penalty is deducted from the 200,000
The region receives nothing, since missing the condition cancels the whole payment
options.misconception: treats a fixed penalty as cancellation of the grant

questions.explanation: The support of 200,000 is reduced by the 100,000 penalty, leaving 100,000 in net support. The penalty is a stated deduction, so it neither falls in a later year nor cancels the payment entirely.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the value of diffuse review
questions.stem: Petition cover sheet, Wyndham: the sheet carries a request that all scrutiny findings be published and that any member may attend any committee. Why would members press for this?

answer.exemplar: Publishing the findings and opening the committees widens the scrutiny, so a decision cannot be examined only by those already inside the system. The point of diffuse review is that more members can look at more decisions, and a published record lets people outside the committee judge the reasoning instead of taking the outcome on trust.

questions.explanation: Open meetings and published findings spread scrutiny beyond a narrow group, which is the value of diffuse review. Keeping committees closed concentrates scrutiny in fewer hands and makes findings unverifiable.
questions.hint: Ask who gains the ability to examine decisions under this proposal.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effects of a packed bench on case outcomes

stimulus.body: The report states that after the appointments were made, the court heard 44 cases in which the government was a party and decided 31 of them in the government's favour. options.text: The change in outcomes proves that every new judge was appointed improperly
options.misconception: treats a pattern in results as proof of illegality

options.text: The government won a smaller share of its cases after the appointments than before
options.misconception: reads a higher win count as a lower success rate

options.misconception: compares the raw counts without converting them to rates

options.text: The government won a larger share of its cases after the appointments than before

questions.explanation: The government won 31 of 44 cases, about 70 percent, after the appointments, against 22 of 40, or 55 percent, before, so its success rate rose. The pattern is strong evidence about the court's composition, not proof of illegality.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Design a defensible performance indicator
questions.stem: Epitome, Thurlby: the society needs one indicator for clear nights a year, and it must be comparable across sites with different skies and different observers. Which indicator meets that requirement?

options.text: The raw count of clear nights logged at each site
options.misconception: ignores that the sites and observers differ from one another

options.text: The percentage of scheduled nights usable for observation, from a shared definition
The number of nights the observer judged clear by personal impression
options.misconception: relies on inconsistent personal judgement between observers

options.text: The number of hours the dome remained open during the year
options.misconception: measures equipment use rather than observing conditions

questions.explanation: A percentage computed from a shared definition of usability is comparable across sites, because it normalises for different skies and observers. Raw counts and personal impressions are not comparable, and dome hours measure equipment rather than conditions.
questions.hint: Choose the measure that is defined the same way everywhere.
